draft.title: Surds
card: A root is a number that, when multiplied by itself the right number of times, gives the number under the root sign. For example, \(\sqrt{25} = 5\) because \(5 \times 5 = 25\).
A surd is a root whose value is not a rational number. Its decimal goes on forever without repeating, so it cannot be written as a fraction of whole numbers.
\(\sqrt{2}\), \(\sqrt{7}\) and \(\sqrt[3]{5}\) are surds. \(\sqrt{9} = 3\) and \(\sqrt[3]{8} = 2\) are not, because they equal whole numbers.
To test a root, ask if the number under the sign is a perfect square (for a square root) or a perfect cube (for a cube root). If it is, the root is not a surd.
draft.remember: A root is a surd only when its value is not a rational number.

a.q: Which of these is a surd?
a.why: 11 is not a perfect square, so \(\sqrt{11}\) is not a rational number. \(\sqrt{49} = 7\), \(\sqrt{0.25} = 0.5\) and \(\sqrt[3]{27} = 3\) all equal rational numbers.
a.clue: Which root does not come out as a neat number?

b.q: Which of these roots is a surd?
b.why: 9 is not a perfect cube, so \(\sqrt[3]{9}\) is not rational. \(\sqrt{64} = 8\), \(\sqrt[3]{64} = 4\) and \(\sqrt{\frac{4}{9}} = \frac{2}{3}\) are all rational. 9 is a perfect square, but this is a cube root, so that does not help.
b.clue: Match the type of root to perfect squares or perfect cubes.

problems.detail: The option \(\sqrt{0.25}\) needs students to see that a decimal can be a perfect square of a rational number (0.5). The card's test only covers perfect squares and cubes of whole numbers, and its examples say non-surds 'equal whole numbers'. A student applying the card's test could wrongly decide \(\sqrt{0.25}\) is a surd.

The option \(\sqrt{\frac{4}{9}}\) needs students to take the root of a fraction (2/3). The card's perfect-square test and its 'equal whole numbers' reason do not cover fractions, so a student following the card could think 4/9 is not a perfect square and call it a surd.

The card says \(\sqrt{9}\) and \(\sqrt[3]{8}\) are not surds 'because they equal whole numbers', which sits uneasily with the definition (not a rational number). The perfect-square/perfect-cube test is given only for whole numbers, yet the questions test decimal and fraction roots.

check.summary: Both answers are correct (\(\sqrt{11}\) and \(\sqrt[3]{9}\)). However, the card's test and its 'whole numbers' reason only cover whole numbers, while each question includes a decimal or fraction root that is rational, so students following the card could be misled.
